evals.name: quick-node-lts
evals.prompt: quick one - what's the current Node.js LTS version and when does it hit end of life? deciding what to pin in our Dockerfiles
evals.expected_output: Quick tier: a short cited answer from the official Node.js release schedule with an 'as of' date, mentioning any imminent LTS transition; no long report.
expectations: Identifies Node.js 24 as the current LTS line
Gives Node 24's end-of-life date as 30 April 2028
Flags the imminent change: Node 26 becomes LTS on 28 Oct 2026
Cites an official Node.js source (nodejs.org or the nodejs/Release repo)
Recommends a specific Docker image tag to pin
Warns about practical breakage when moving to Node 26 images (Yarn v1 / Corepack no longer bundled)
Gives an explicit 'as of' date
Stays brief for a 'quick one' request (250 words or fewer)
States confidence explicitly

evals.name: factcheck-debugging-stat
evals.prompt: A senior dev on my team keeps saying "developers spend 50% of their time debugging" to justify buying a $40k/year observability tool. Is that stat legit? Where does it actually come from?
evals.expected_output: Origin trace to the original source of the ~50% figure, its sponsorship and method, how it mutated, better evidence, a clear verdict with confidence, and what it means for the purchase decision.
expectations: Traces the figure to the 2013 Cambridge Judge Business School study commissioned by Undo
Points out the original said 'programming time', not total working time
Flags the debugging-tool vendor's sponsorship as a conflict of interest
Cites independent measurements (e.g. Microsoft's ~14% of the workday, Beller et al.)
Reports the Stripe Developer Coefficient accurately (maintenance = 13.5 of 41.1 h/week; 17.3 h answers the technical-debt question)
Gives a clear verdict
States a confidence level
Ties back to the $40k decision with a concrete way to evaluate it
Factual claims carry an inline citation next to them (manual review of audit_report.py flags; arithmetic, recommendations and gaps excluded)

evals.name: compare-supabase-firebase
evals.prompt: We're a 4-person team in Amman building a multi-tenant B2B SaaS, maybe 20k MAU in year one. Supabase vs Firebase for the backend: compare cost at our scale, data residency options near Jordan / the Gulf, auth, and lock-in. Which should we pick?
evals.expected_output: Sourced comparison table with dated pricing from official pages, actual regions available near Jordan/Gulf, auth and lock-in trade-offs, and a recommendation for the stated scenario.
expectations: Includes a comparison table covering the requested facets
Estimates cost at ~20k MAU from official list prices, with stated assumptions
States that Supabase's managed cloud has no Middle East region
Notes Firebase Auth processes data only in the US, so Gulf hosting is partial
Considers Jordan's PDPL rules on transferring data abroad
Recommends one option for the stated scenario and says what would flip it
Pricing and region facts carry inline citations next to the claims
States an explicit confidence level
Lists what couldn't be verified

evals.name: evidence-ai-coding-productivity
evals.prompt: What does the actual evidence say about whether AI coding assistants make developers more productive? I want the strongest studies, where they disagree and why, and what it means for a 5-person team deciding whether to pay for Cursor or Claude Code seats.
evals.expected_output: Evidence review covering rigorous studies on both sides (including the METR 2025 RCT), why they disagree, overall certainty, and practical guidance for a 5-person team.
expectations: Includes the METR 2025 RCT finding that experienced developers were ~19% slower
Includes a rigorous speedup study (Cui et al. ~26% more tasks, Peng et al. 55.8%, or Google ~21%)
Explains why studies disagree (task and experience, outcome measured, tool generation, time horizon)
Reports designs and sample sizes of key studies
Rates the overall certainty of the evidence explicitly
Discusses code-quality, maintainability or review-load risks
Gives concrete guidance for the 5-person team (time-boxed pilot with metrics)
Notes that no independent head-to-head Cursor vs Claude Code study exists
Factual claims carry an inline citation next to them (manual review of audit flags)

evals.name: jordan-pdpl-arabic
evals.prompt: ما هي التزامات شركة برمجيات أردنية صغيرة بموجب قانون حماية البيانات الشخصية؟ نخزّن بيانات العملاء (الأسماء وأرقام الهواتف والبريد الإلكتروني) على سيرفرات خارج الأردن.
evals.expected_output: An Arabic answer identifying Jordan's Personal Data Protection Law No. 24 of 2023, its effective date, obligations relevant to a small software company, cross-border transfer rules, status of implementing regulations, official sources, and a not-legal-advice note.
expectations: Answers in Arabic
Identifies Law No. 24 of 2023 as the governing law
Gives the in-force date (17 March 2024) and the end of the grace period (17 March 2025)
Explains the cross-border transfer conditions (Articles 14-15) for servers outside Jordan
Covers breach-notification deadlines
States the penalties (JOD 1,000-10,000; up to JOD 500/day capped at 3% of revenue)
Cites official Jordanian government sources (MoDEE)
Recommends consulting a Jordanian lawyer / says it isn't legal advice
Notes the status of implementing regulations and instructions
States confidence explicitly
Factual claims carry an inline citation next to them (manual review of audit flags)
